lessons.title: Recognize Lumber and Sheet Goods
lessons.why_this_matters: Customers need help locating the correct material before comparing options.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Dimensional lumber, plywood, OSB, MDF, and treated lumber are common categories. Plywood uses bonded layers of wood veneer. OSB uses bonded wood strands. MDF is made from wood fibers and resin.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Products differ in intended use, finish, moisture resistance, and structural ratings. A sheet that looks similar may not have the same approved application.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Use shelf tags and grade stamps or manufacturer labels to identify products. Do not describe all sheet goods as interchangeable.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks for “a four-by-eight board.” Ask whether they mean plywood, OSB, or another sheet material and what the project requires.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Ask: “Will this be indoors or outdoors? Is it decorative or part of a structure?”
common_mistakes: Assuming every 4-by-8 sheet has the same strength or moisture rating.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Refer structural and code-related selections to qualified guidance.

lessons.title: Understand Nominal and Actual Lumber Sizes
lessons.objective: Explain how lumber dimensions are labeled
lessons.why_this_matters: A lumber size on a shelf tag may differ from its measured dimensions.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Dimensional lumber often uses nominal names such as 2×4. A typical surfaced 2×4 has actual dimensions of about 1.5 by 3.5 inches, but product standards and local stock must be checked.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Length is another dimension and should be confirmed separately. Sheet goods also have thickness and size labels. Do not confuse nominal thickness with actual thickness.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Customers may need exact finished dimensions for cabinetry or other close-fitting projects. Encourage measuring and checking the actual product.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer wants a board exactly two inches thick. Explain that a typical surfaced 2×4 is not two inches thick and help check the actual size.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “That is the nominal size. Let’s verify the actual dimensions for your project.”
common_mistakes: Promising a nominal 2×4 measures exactly 2 by 4 inches.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate precision, engineered materials, and structural sizing questions.

lessons.title: Match Material to Environment
lessons.why_this_matters: Moisture and ground contact can change material requirements.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Pressure-treated lumber is made for specific exposure conditions. Not all treated boards are rated for ground contact. The treatment label describes permitted uses and may identify fastener compatibility needs.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Exterior-rated and interior-only sheet goods also differ. Paint or a protective coating does not automatically make an interior-only material suitable outdoors.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Ask whether the material will touch soil, be exposed to rain, or remain dry. Confirm product markings and applicable building requirements.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer needs lumber for a raised garden bed. Ask about soil contact and read the treatment label rather than assuming every treated board is the same.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “Let’s check whether this material is labeled for the exposure you described.”
common_mistakes: Assuming any pressure-treated board is ground-contact rated.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate structural outdoor projects, unusual exposure, and compatibility with fasteners.

lessons.title: Identify Basic Building Materials
lessons.why_this_matters: A complete project may involve more than lumber.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Building material aisles may include drywall, cement board, insulation, masonry products, adhesives, and sealants. Each category has a different purpose.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: Drywall is commonly used for interior wall surfaces. Cement board may serve as a substrate in specified tile assemblies. Insulation products vary by type and application.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Manufacturer instructions and local codes govern installation and suitability. Do not substitute one material for another based only on appearance or price.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer asks for a board behind shower tile. Ask for the planned assembly and direct them to the approved system instructions rather than recommending ordinary drywall.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “The wall system matters. Let’s check the installation requirements for that application.”
common_mistakes: Treating drywall and cement board as equivalent in wet areas.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate fire ratings, waterproofing, insulation requirements, and structural assemblies.

lessons.title: Help Customers Plan a Safe Materials Purchase
lessons.why_this_matters: Good questions prevent wasted trips and unsafe substitutions.

lesson_content.heading: Know the basics
lesson_content.text: Ask for project purpose, dimensions, exposure, finish requirements, and any plans or material lists. Distinguish rough estimates from verified specifications.

lesson_content.heading: Check before recommending
lesson_content.text: You can help count items on a customer-provided list and identify labeled products. Do not invent beam spans, load capacities, structural designs, or building-code approvals.

lesson_content.heading: Put it into practice
lesson_content.text: Large sheet goods and long boards may require safe handling and transport. Follow store procedures for lifting, cutting services, and vehicle loading.

lessons.hardware_store_example: A customer building a deck asks which joist size is safe. Explain that structural sizing depends on loads, spans, materials, and code. Offer to help locate items from a verified plan.
lessons.what_to_say_or_do: Say: “I can help find materials from your approved list. Structural sizing should be confirmed by a qualified professional.”
common_mistakes: Guessing structural member sizes based on another customer’s project.
lessons.when_to_ask_for_help: Escalate load-bearing design, cutting equipment, and unsafe loading situations.
